study_type.claude: Quasi-experiment (exploratory, cross-sectional, natural quasi-experiment via survey)
study_type.note: Survey-based comparison of non-randomized Copilot users vs non-users.

research_method.claude: Exploratory cross-sectional natural quasi-experiment; survey of 57 questions (mostly 5-point Likert) comparing Copilot users and non-users; Top 2-Box; one-sided Mann-Whitney U with RBC and CLES; Bonferroni p < 0.0056; items adapted from GitHub Research's SPACE-based survey
research_method.nlm: Exploratory cross-sectional natural quasi-experiment; 57-item online survey; Top 2-Box; Mann-Whitney U, RBC, CLES; Bonferroni-corrected threshold
research_method.value: Exploratory, cross-sectional natural quasi-experiment (non-randomized users vs non-users of GitHub Copilot); 57-question survey, mostly 5-point Likert, items adapted from GitHub Research's survey; Top 2-Box analysis and one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with rank-biserial correlation and CLES, Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.0056 over 9 hypotheses

context.nlm: Industry / public sector, NAV Norway, IT department ~1000 employees; 115 participants (67 users, 48 non-users)

evidence.quote: The research design can be described as an exploratory, cross-sectional, natural quasi-experiment involving two distinct groups: users and non-users of Copilot in NAV.
evidence.loc: PDF p. 2 (2 Method and Study Design)

evidence.quote: we employed the nonparametric Mann-Whitney U Test [9] to assess differences between the groups' distributions, complemented by the Rank-Biserial Correlation (RBC) [7] and the Common Language Effect Size (CLES) [10] for evaluating effect magnitude.
The final questionnaire consisted of 57 questions (28 for both groups and an additional 29 for the users), most of them being 5-point Likert Agreement scale-type questions.
NAV has about 1000 employees in their IT department, and the teams follow agile principles of software development.
The final survey collected a total of 115 responses, comprising 67 users and 48 non-users of GitHub Copilot.

Findings reveal that Copilot users experience significantly greater focus on engaging tasks and less dependence on colleagues compared to non-users, while non-users maintain a more cautious stance on AI use in the public sector.
This confirmed our hypothesis, with nearly half of the users disagreeing with the notion that they rely on assistance or guidance from colleagues, compared to just a fifth of the non-users.
Users also reported a notably higher job satisfaction than the non-users, with 87% of the users agreeing that they felt satisfied in their job, as compared to 73% of the non-users.
